title: Council Post: Automation For The Things You Can’t Possibly Anticipate
text:
Malinka Waliyadde is co-founder & CEO of AKASA, the first Unified Automation™ company for revenue cycle management in healthcare.
There are three tiers on the scale of knowledge and ignorance: the “known knowns,” or the problems you’re aware of and know how to solve; the “known unknowns,” or the problems you’re aware of but the solution may be unclear; and the “unknown unknowns,” or the problems you simply can’t anticipate.
We all know which one is the most dangerous — to both organizations and individuals. Automation approaches and technologies have evolved over the past decade or so to handle these categories of knowledge differently. One basic technology, robotic process automation (RPA), can handle the known knowns quite well, while machine learning can help respond to and analyze the known unknowns more effectively.
But people, with all their intuition for handling complexity, are best at identifying the unknown unknowns — the unexpected outliers. Demands on automation tools and technology are only going to get more complex. It’s going to revolve around solving for the known unknowns and unknown unknowns. Depending too heavily on RPA to respond to unknowns can lead to a vicious cycle: the outlier comes down the chain, the RPA fails to identify it and respond appropriately, and the system breaks.
Here at AKASA, we’ve helped our healthcare customers in revenue cycle management (RCM) identify and manage unknowns through our expert-in-the-loop solution. It's an antifragile system that leads instead to a virtuous cycle of converting the unknown to known, in which the human expert handles the outlier, the AI learns and adapts from observing the human expert, and then the AI manages the former outlier appropriately in the future.
From a design standpoint, building an expert-in-the-loop approach to automation that is capable of adapting to unknowns presents an enormous engineering challenge. It requires untangling four distinct problems — all of which will likely exist for any automation platform that integrates AI with human experts. Here’s how to solve those problems:
1. Balancing AI Confidence
Engineering the AI to accurately gauge its ability to recognize and handle difficult or unknown tasks is paramount. If the AI doesn’t have enough confidence to manage such tasks, it will bump too many of them to human experts, greatly reducing system efficiency. An overconfident AI, on the other hand, will attempt to tackle unknown outliers it can’t handle, breaking the system or incorrectly handling the task.
2. Triaging Outliers Efficiently
Healthcare is all about the outliers and edge cases that we don’t see coming. The AI must be designed to swiftly triage tasks outside its capability to human experts — without interrupting its regular workflow. Automation systems that rely on basic RPA technology would break in these instances and related work would come to a halt until the bot has been reprogrammed. But AI-based automation systems with the built-in ability to triage outliers to human experts are more flexible. That flexibility is the key to building an autonomous solution that can handle unknowns and work without interruption.
3. Giving Human Experts X-Ray Vision Into The AI’s Brain
Through an intuitive head-up display, human experts in the loop must have direct and ready oversight of the entire AI process, allowing them to observe, assess and either approve or reject the AI’s proposed actions on a very granular level. All in a time frame of minutes or less. Without such oversight capability, resolution of unknown outliers could take hours or days.
4. Enabling Continuous Learning
The AI must be designed to continuously observe, learn and adapt, shadowing human experts in a kind of running apprenticeship. This learning and adaptation must continue indefinitely as the AI becomes more and more capable of handling complex tasks, persistently transforming the outlier into the ordinary — the unknown into the known. Today’s outliers become tomorrow’s built-in solutions.
“You don’t know what you don’t know” is only the starting condition. With close analysis and insight, you can identify what you don’t know — and what it’s costing you and your customers. Then it’s one step closer to becoming the known known — or knowledge you can bank on. Effective, carefully designed automation helps us better find and illuminate the unknown unknowns.

title: Synopsys, Cadence, Google And NVIDIA All Agree: Use AI To Help Design Chips
text:
Synopsys created a buzz in 2020, and now Google, NVIDIA, and Cadence Design have joined the party. What lies ahead?
Introduction
Designing modern semiconductors can take years and scores of engineers armed with state-of-the-art EDA design tools. But the semiconductor landscape and the world around us is being revolutionized by hundreds of new chips, primarily driven by AI. Some entrepreneurial thought leaders believe that the expensive and lengthy chip design process could shrink from 2-3 years to 2-3 months if hardware development was to become more agile, more autonomous. And chief among a new breed of agile design tools is AI itself.
The Semiconductor Design Landscape
This discussion began in earnest when the EDA leader Synopsys announced DSO.ai, Design Space Optimization AI, an software product that could more autonomously identify optimal ways to arrange silicon components (layouts) on a chip to reduce the area and reduce power consumption, even while increasing performance. Using reinforcement learning, DSO.ai could evaluate billions of alternatives against design goals, and produce a design that was significantly better than that produced by talented engineers. The size of the problem/solution space DSO.ai addresses is staggering: there are something like 1090,000 possible ways to place components on a chip. That compares to 10360 possible moves in the game of Go which was mastered by Google AI in 2016. Since reinforcement learning can play Go better than the world champion, one could conceivably design a better chip if one is willing to spend the compute time to do it.
Results are quite impressive, realizing 18% faster operating frequency at 21% lower power, while reducing engineering time from six months to as little as one. In a recent interview, Synopsys’ Founder and Co-CEO Aart de Geus disclosed that Samsung have a working chip in-house today that was designed with DSO.ai. This would indeed be the world’s first use of AI to create a chip layout in production – from RTL to tapeout.
Recently Google published results of doing something similar, as has NVIDIA. And Cadence Design Systems just announced an AI-based optimization platform similar to Synopsys DSO.ai. Before we take a look at these efforts, lets back up a little and look at the entire semiconductor design space. A good place to start is the Gajski-Kuhn Chart that outlines all the steps of chip design along three axes: the Behavioral level where architects defines what the chip is supposed to do, the Structural level where they determine how the chip is organized, and the Geometry level where engineers define how the chip is laid out.
Based on this model, each step towards the center (which is when the team “tapes out” the chip to the fabrication partner) feeds the work in the next phase in a clockwise direction. To date, all the application of AI has been in the geometry space, or physical design, to address the waning of Moore’s Law.
Synopsys DSO.ai
As I covered at launch, Synopsys DSO.ai was the first entrant to apply AI to the physical design process, producing floor plans that consumed lower power, ran at higher frequencies, and occupied less space than the best an experienced design could produce. What really attracted my attention was the profound effect of AI on productivity; DSO.ai users were able to achieve in a few days what it used to take teams of experts, many weeks.
Google Research and NVIDIA Research
Both companies have produced research papers that describe the use of reinforcement learning to assist in the physical design of the floor plan. In Google’s case, AI is being used to lay out the floor plan of the next generation TPU Chip and the company is investigating additional uses of AI such as in architectural optimization.
NVIDIA similarly has focused on that same low-hanging fruit: floorplanning, and with all the compute capacity they have in-house, I’d expect NVDIA to continue to eat their own dogfood and use AI to design better AI chips.
Cadence Design Systems Enters the Market
Cadence has recently launched their “intelligent chip explorer” called Cerebrus to optimize the physical design process with reinforcement learning. Not to be confused with the Wafer Scale Engine AI maker “Cerebras”, the newly announced platform looks similar in capability to the DSO.ai that Synopsys launched in March 2020, focusing on physical design. While Google and NVIDIA may have sufficient resources and skills to develop their own AI for design optimization, the majority of semiconductor companies and projects will select a tool from an EDA vendor. Cadence’s entrance seems to solidify the reinforcement learning technique as the next big shift in design methodology. We believe AI will become pervasive as designers become more comfortable with letting the machine determine the layout, and competitive pressures mount.
Conclusions and Outlook
The excellent research being conducted at NVIDIA and Google will reinforce the message to designers that they should rapidly consider AI-led optimization to improve performance, cost, and energy consumption. NVIDIA and Google are undoubtably focusing this effort to produce better GPU’s and Cloud TPU platforms to enhance their competitive position. We think rumors to the effect that these companies might enter the EDA tools market are off base: the AI optimization is a tool they use to help improve their own products and services.
Cadence Design System’s entry has validated the approach as well, and the industry momentum will now accelerate. However, Cadence is just beginning the journey, while Synopsys enjoys the pole position, with at least a full year head start: Synopsys customers such as Samsung already taping out designs that were created with DSO.ai.
Now the question becomes, what about “The Rest of the Story”? Using AI in physical design is great, but in our view, it is only the beginning, representing perhaps only 10% of the opportunity. There are rich fields to harvest along the Behavior and Structure axes, which will create a spiral of optimization across the design workflow. We look forward to hearing what Synopsys co-CEO Aart de Geus has to say on this topic when he presents the Keynote speech at the upcoming HotChips conference on August 23.
Stay tuned!

text:
Last week saw mixed performance from the markets as the days unfolded, with the ADP’s nonfarm jobs report, Thursday’s unemployment report, and a new 60-day moratorium on evictions all playing on investors’ hopes and fears.
Friday’s Labor Department report seemed to assuage some of investors’ burgeoning concerns, however. The government reported July nonfarm payroll jobs increased 943,000 in July, topping the Dow Jones estimate of 845,000.
Additionally, the unemployment rate slid down to 5.4% compared to expectations around 5.7%. The fastest-growing sectors for the month proved no surprise in the wake of the reopening economy: leisure and hospitality. These were followed closely behind by education, professional, and business-related services. And to top off a report mostly filled with (mostly) good news, average hourly earnings rose around 0.4% throughout the month.
Through it all, our artificial intelligence algorithms plucked out the stocks that appeared to trend in investors’ portfolios, the news, and on the back of these economic reports. And now, we’re bringing you a high-level summary of which stocks trended and why – as well as which stocks will continue to trend in the coming trading sessions.

Novavax, In (NVAX)
Novavax, Inc
Novavax investors have weathered some wild swings in the last six months as the company – which, despite the name, has never released a vaccine in its 30-year history – has tried, failed, and tried again to push out a Covid-19 vaccine of any description.
Last week, Novavax took one step closer to inoculating its first customer post-trial for the first time in its 30-year history as the biotech firm struck a deal with the European Union to provide up to 200 million coronavirus vaccine doses (pending regulatory approval). While it’s still in the early stages, this new partnership made Novavax a promising candidate to become the fourth Covid-19 vaccine approved in the United States, as well.
Unfortunately, the stock’s good news was short-lived, as Friday saw Novavax delay its U.S. Covid-19 vaccine submission to the FDA for the third time. The company now says it expects to apply for U.S. emergency authorization in Q4, despite already filing in regions like India, Indonesia, and the Philippines, as well as the E.U.
Additionally, the company’s Q2 earnings results came as a disappointing shock to investors, touting a loss of $4.75 per share compared to an expected loss of $3.63. Moreover, Q2 revenue came in almost $100 million below estimates at $298 million for the quarter.
Over the last three fiscal years, Novavax’s revenue exploded almost 3,350% as it climbed from $34.3 million to $475.6 million. In the same period, operating income soared 434% to $414 million compared to $174 million. That said, per-share earnings dropped from $9.99 to $7.27.
Currently, Novavax’s revenue is expected to skyrocket in the ballpark of 88% in the next 12 months. But at its current price and volatility, our AI rates Novavax a no-go, with a C in Technicals, D in Quality Value, and Fs in Growth and Low Volatility Momentum.
The Boeing Company (BA)
The Boeing Company nicked up 0.6% to $231.33 per share on Friday. The company’s stock changed hands around 6.1 million times in the trading session to a price well above its 22-day average of $226 and change. Currently, Boeing trends up 8% for the year at a 12-month P/E of 62.5x.
Boeing enjoyed a spot on our trending lists last week after announcing its Q2 2021 earnings results, which found that the battered and beleaguered airplane manufacturer managed to pull a profit for the first time in nearly two years. The company’s sudden tailwind came about as a result of surging commercial plane orders and deliveries, which in turn occurred as airlines attempt to update their fleets and meet renewed travel demand.
All told, Boeing reported $567 million in profits compared to a YOY loss of $2.96 billion. Additionally, revenue topped analyst estimates to end the quarter with $17 billion in cash flow, with the company logging 40 cents per share profit versus an 83-cent loss this time last year.
In more recent happenings, Boeing’s made our trending list this week on a variety of mixed news. For instance, the company’s Starliner capsule, which was expected to launch on Tuesday, had to be wheeled back inside the assembly hangar to troubleshoot some “misbehaving” valves. If a quick fix isn’t underway, the company will have to disassemble the rocket to locate the problem. And in unrelated news, the FAA issued Boeing a new safety directive on Thursday to address potential fire suppression safety issues in its 7373 Next Generation and MAX jets.
Over the last few fiscal years, Boeing’s revenue has plunged by almost half, from $101 billion three years ago to $58 billion in the most recent year. Operating income followed suit, dropping from $11.8 billion to just under $8.66 billion. That said, per-share earnings jumped over three dollars from $17.85 to $20.88 during the pandemic year.
All told, Boeing is expected to see forward 12-month revenue growth around 17%. Our AI rates this airplane manufacturer C in Technicals, D in Low Volatility Momentum, and F in Growth and Quality Value.
Activision Blizzard, Inc (ATVI)
Activision Blizzard, Inc. popped 2.6% to $82.43 on Friday, closing out the day with 9.7 million trades on the docket. The stock currently trades down 11.2% for the year at a forward 12-month P/E of 21.8x.
Activision Blizzard splashed onto our trending lists in a big way last week. While we might have expected this video game developer to show up due to its quarterly earnings call – which reported 19% revenue growth in a spot of what the company hoped would be good news – overwhelmingly, Activision Blizzard’s appearance was marred by scandal.
Last week, news outlets reported that the state of California filed a gender-bias lawsuit against the company on allegations that it promoted a “frat boy” culture where women and marginalized groups are sexually harassed, underpaid, and passed over for promotions. The lawsuit – and its aftermath – prompted an exodus of executives from their high-level positions in the company.
One of the first to leave was president for corporate affairs Frances Townsend, who stepped down as executive sponsor of the ABK’s Women’s Network after calling the allegations “distorted” and “false.” She also tweeted a link to an article titled “The Problem with Whistleblowing” before deleting her social media account. And on 3 August, both president of Blizzard studios J. Allen Brack and senior vice president of global human resources Jesse Meschuk left their positions.
But how this lawsuit will affect the future of the company – and its bottom line – remains to be seen. Over the last three fiscal years, Activision Blizzard saw revenue growth of 19.2%, climbing from $7.5 billion to almost $8.1 billion. In the same period, operating income surged 62% from just under $2 billion to $2.83 billion. Meanwhile, per-share earnings jumped to $2.82 compared to $2.40 three years prior, though return on equity slipped from 17.7% to 15.8%.
All told, Activision Blizzard’s forward 12-month revenue is expected to inch up around 0.3%. Our AI rates this company as a slightly above-average investment, with As in Low Volatility Momentum and Quality Value and Cs in Technicals and Growth.
Facebook, Inc (FB)
Facebook, Inc nudged up 0.15% to $363.51 on Friday, trading 8.9 million shares to a price $9 over the 22-day average. The stock sits up 33% YTD and trades at 25.6x forward earnings.
Facebook trended last week as part of the tech sector’s rise, fueled in part by concerns of the delta variant’s impact on the return-to-work economy. The company’s 28 July Q2 2021 earnings call also applied upward pressure as the social media giant reported a substantial $29 billion in revenue for the quarter at $3.61 in per-share profits. Management also warned investors to expect headwinds in the latter half of 2021 growth decelerates against last year’s performance.
Facebook holds its trending status again this week after rolling out a new prayer request feature in an effort to reach out to faith-holding communities. While the new tool already has privacy skeptics worried about its impact, the social media giant reports that advertisers won’t be able to use prayer posts to target ads.
That leads us to another reason Facebook continues to trend: its ban of NYU researchers seeking to understand how political ads and misinformation target users and spread across the digital ecosystem. Although Facebook claims the company suspended accounts in line with its FTC-ordered privacy program, the FTC released a letter stating that it “supports efforts to shed light on opaque business practices.”
Over the last several fiscal years, Facebook’s revenue has leapt almost 88% to almost $86 billion compared to $55.8 billion three years prior. Operating income saw similar growth of 79% as it climbed from $24.9 billion to $32.67 billion. Additionally, per-share earnings soared 78% to $10.09 compared to $7.57 three years earlier, though return on equity fell from 28% to 25.4%.
Currently, Facebook is expected to see around 7.5% revenue growth over the next 12 months. Our AI rates this social media company just above average, with Bs in Technicals, Growth, and Quality Value, and a C in Low Volatility Momentum.
General Motors Company (GM)
General Motors Company closed up 1.1% on Friday, trading 14.97 million shares to a final price of $55.05. The stock sits up 32.2% for the year and trades at 9.4x forward earnings.
GM hit our trending lists last week thanks to the release of its Q2 2021 earnings report – though it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows for the famed automaker. Admittedly, the company raked in $34.2 billion in revenue to beat the $30.9 billion consensus, as well as a net income of $2.8 billion in the quarter compared to the YOY $758 million loss.
But some investors traded up a storm – and drove the share price down – upon seeing its underwhelming $1.97 in per-share earnings, which came in 26 cents below estimates. Management attributed its performance to $1.3 billion in warranty recall costs, $800 million of which came from addressing its Chevrolet Bolt EV fire risk.
However, this quarter may mark a turning point for the automaker after seeing its revenue plunge from $147 billion three years ago to $122 billion in the most recent fiscal year, with per-share earnings dropped a dollar-twenty to $4.33. Return on equity fell, too, from 20.5% to 13.2%. That said, operating income actually saw growth of 139% to $8.56 billion compared to $6.29 billion in the three-year period.
Currently, General Motors is expected to experience around 8.2% revenue growth in the next year. Our AI rates this automotive company solidly average, with Cs across the board in Technicals, Growth, Low Volatility Momentum, and Quality Value.
